references.text: God prevents humanity from eating from the tree of life after the fall, and they are expelled from Eden's garden with cherubim guarding the way to the tree.
God grants humanity freedom to eat from every tree in the garden but forbids them from eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, with death as the consequence.
The tree of life appears again in the new Jerusalem, standing beside the river of the water of life, bearing fruit twelve times a year for the healing of the nations.
Those who wash their robes gain the right to the tree of life and to enter through the gates into the city—an eschatological fulfillment of what began in Eden's garden.
Jesus promises the one who overcomes that they may eat from the tree of life in God's paradise, a direct link to the tree of life that stood in the midst of Eden's garden.
Wisdom is described as a tree of life (עֵץ־חַיִּים) for those who grasp it—the same expression used for the tree in Eden's garden.
Jeremiah compares the one who trusts in the Lord to a tree planted by water that always bears fruit—an image reflecting the trees God caused to grow in Eden's garden.
Ezekiel describes trees in God's garden (Eden) as beautiful and envied, echoing the description of the trees that were pleasing to look at in Eden's garden.
A direct continuation of the same event: the presentation of the trees and God's command regarding what is permitted to eat.
A direct consequence of the action: the loss of access to the tree of life mentioned in 2:9.
A direct reference to the description in 2:9: sin distorts God's good creation by focusing on the tree as 'beautiful' and 'good for food'.
